newsitem.title: JAPAN: More Japanese to travel abroad, but more frugally.
newsitem.headline: More Japanese to travel abroad, but more frugally.

text.p: A record number of Japanese will spend their summer holidays this year in overseas destinations like Maui and Milan, but they are not likely to splurge on lavish dinners or expensive souvenirs, industry experts said.
Japan's largest tourist agency, Japan Travel Bureau (JTB), said it expects a record 3.19 million Japanese to travel abroad in July and August, up 1.9 percent from a year earlier.
"Overseas travel has reached a point of stable growth, but spending is likely to be restrained this year," JTB spokesman Toshihiro Ebana said on Friday.

For years, the Japanese craving for gourmet meals and brand-name goods overseas has helped narrow Japan's current account surplus against other countries, but industry experts predict that purse strings will tighten in 1997.

Japan's balance of payments in its current account was 7.16 trillion yen ($61.7 billion) in 1996, while the largest travel balance deficit was with the United States at 952.1 billion yen ($8.20 billion), Japan's Finance Ministry said.
Each Japanese tourist abroad this summer is expected to spend an average of 291,000 yen ($2,508), up a meagre one percent from last year, JTB said.
Japanese tourists have generally become more price conscious since the bursting of Japan's asset price bubble in the early 1990s, travel agencies said.
In addition, a rise in the nationwide consumption tax in April and the cancellation of a special reduction in income taxes at home have left Japanese tourists with less to spend abroad.

A recent decline in the value of the yen would also discourage spending abroad, said Peter Morgan, senior economist at HSBC James Capel. When the yen is weak, Japanese tourists have to put up more yen for goods and services abroad.
"The weak yen will discourage overseas travel and the deregulation of domestic air fares will encourage domestic travel," Morgan said.
Domestic travel in July and August is expected to grow 2.9 percent year-on-year, rising faster than overseas travel for the first time in six years, JTB spokeswoman Yuri Sakamoto said.
She added that an increasing number of price-conscious Japanese travellers has shifted their holidays to June and September, when tour prices are lower.

Major carriers Japan Airlines Co Ltd and All Nippon Airways Co Ltd, as well as JTB, said the most sought-after overseas destination this summer among Japanese is the United States, as it has been for the past several years.
As many as 618,000 Japanese will descend on Hawaii, California and other U.S. locations in July and August, JTB said.
The second-most popular destination is Western Europe, JTB said, and Italy leads with cities such as Rome and Milan luring young Japanese women with popular cuisines and designer brands.
Although the number of Japanese holidaymakers heading for Asia is relatively small, it is growing rapidly, JTB said.
Hong Kong, however, is an exception.
In July and August, Japanese visitors to Hong Kong, the hottest destination before the handover to China on July 1, are expected to drop 45 percent from last year, JTB said.
JTB's Sakamoto said, however, that the former British colony will regain momentum as long as Japanese tourists are able to shop and enjoy good Chinese food there.

"The sudden drop in interest in Hong Kong is a reaction to the hype that preceded the handover. But there are new attractions that will bring back Japanese tourists in the future, with next year's opening of a new airport and new hotels," she added.
